entry: Flag carrier airline of the United Kingdom, based in London. Formed on March 31, 1974, by merging British Overseas Airways Corporation, British European Airways and two regional carriers, it was privatized in February 1987. In January 2011 it merged with Iberia to create the International Airlines Group (IAG), a holding company registered in [[Madrid]]. Its main hub is at [[Heathrow Airport]]. During the [[COVID-19]] crisis it received a bailout equivalent to £300 million.

Westernmost province of Canada, lying in the [[Pacific Northwest]] between the Pacific Ocean and the Rocky Mountains. Its capital is Victoria on [[Vancouver Island]], and [[Vancouver]] is the largest city. The population was estimated at 5.68 million in 2025. Indigenous peoples have lived in the area for at least 10,000 years. The Colony of British Columbia was founded in 1858 in response to the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush, and the province entered Confederation in 1871 as the sixth province of Canada. The economy rests on [[Forestry]], mining, [[Filmmaking]], tourism and [[Real estate]].

British colony in East Asia (1841–1997). Hong Kong Island was occupied in 1841 and ceded to Britain in perpetuity under the Treaty of Nanking of 1842, which followed the [[First Opium War]]. The Kowloon Peninsula was added in 1860, and the New Territories were leased for 99 years in 1898. The [[Empire of Japan]] occupied the territory from 1941 to 1945. Under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration, Britain agreed to return the territory to China, which took place in July 1997, when Hong Kong became a special administrative region.

British Overseas Territory in the Indian Ocean, comprising seven [[Atoll|atolls]] of the Chagos Archipelago with a total land area of 60 square kilometres (23 square miles). The largest island, [[Diego Garcia]], hosts a joint military facility of the United Kingdom and the United States. Britain separated the archipelago from the Crown Colony of [[Mauritius]] in 1965. Between 1968 and 1973 the Chagossians, then about 2,000 people, were expelled to Mauritius and Seychelles, and the British government has repeatedly denied them the right of return. Mauritius claims sovereignty, and a 2019 advisory opinion of the [[International Court of Justice]] called for the islands to be given to Mauritius. A 2025 treaty would have transferred sovereignty to Mauritius while leasing the Diego Garcia base to Britain for 99 years, but its ratification was suspended after backlash from U.S. President [[Donald Trump]] in 2026.

Archipelago in the North Atlantic Ocean off the northwestern coast of continental Europe, comprising Great Britain, Ireland, the Isle of Man, the Hebrides, the Northern Isles and over 6,000 smaller islands. It covers 315,159 sq km and has a combined population of almost 75 million. It includes two sovereign states, the Republic of Ireland and the United Kingdom. Ben Nevis, the highest mountain, rises to 1,345 metres (4,413 ft). Great Britain became an island by 7000 BC with the flooding of [[Doggerland]]. The term is geographical rather than political, and the Government of Ireland does not officially recognise it.

National library of the United Kingdom, based in London. Created on July 1, 1973, under the British Library Act 1972, it was separated from the [[British Museum]], which had held the national library's collections. As a legal deposit library, it receives copies of all books produced in the United Kingdom and Ireland. Its collection is estimated at over 200 million items, including around 14 million books, and it adds about three million items each year. The purpose-built building beside St Pancras station was officially opened by [[Elizabeth II]] on June 25, 1998. Off-site storage is at Boston Spa in Yorkshire.

Public museum of human history, art and culture in the Bloomsbury area of London. Established by Act of Parliament in 1753, it was the world's first public national museum and opened to the public in 1759 at Montagu House. Its foundations lie in the collection of the Anglo-Irish physician Sir Hans Sloane. The permanent collection of eight million artefacts is the largest in the world, and the museum received 6,440,120 visitors in 2025. Some of its best-known acquisitions, including the Greek Elgin Marbles and the Egyptian [[Rosetta Stone]], are subject to long-term disputes and repatriation claims. Like all UK national museums, it charges no admission fee except for loan exhibitions.

Fourteen dependent territories of the United Kingdom that lie outside the British Islands. They are remnants of the British Empire that remained under British sovereignty after decolonisation, with varying constitutional statuses. The UK retains authority over defence, foreign relations and internal security, and all fourteen recognise the British monarch as head of state. The population is about 250,000, with the Cayman Islands and [[Bermuda]] accounting for about half of it. Three territories, including the [[British Indian Ocean Territory]], have no permanent civilian population.

Period of Crown rule in India, from 1858 to 1947, when the British Crown governed the Indian subcontinent. It was instituted on June 28, 1858, after the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]] transferred power from the [[East India Company]] to the Crown. Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. Directly administered areas were called British India, while the princely states were ruled by indigenous rulers under British paramountcy. The Raj covered almost all of present-day [[India]], [[Pakistan]], Bangladesh and [[Myanmar]]. In 1947 it was partitioned into the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan. Its economic legacy, including the so-called drain of wealth to Britain, is debated.

British Overseas Territory in the Caribbean, consisting of Tortola, Virgin Gorda, Anegada, Jost Van Dyke and more than 50 smaller islands and cays. The capital, Road Town, is on Tortola. The population was 28,054 at the 2010 census and was estimated at 38,984 in 2024. The economy is dominated by tourism and financial services, and the territory uses the United States dollar. Its financial services sector is known as a hub for tax evasion and concealment of assets. British Virgin Islanders have been British citizens since 2002.

English and later British settlement of North America, the Caribbean and parts of Central and South America, from the late 16th century. Sir Walter Raleigh established the short-lived [[Roanoke Colony]] in 1585. The first permanent English colony in the Americas was founded at [[Jamestown]], Virginia, in 1607, and the English later established colonies in the Caribbean, including [[Barbados]] and [[Jamaica]]. The [[Hudson's Bay Company]] established Rupert's Land in the Hudson Bay drainage basin. Britain took the French colony of Canada and the Floridas in 1763, but most North American colonies gained independence through the [[American Revolutionary War]], which ended in 1783. Britain continued to colonize in the 19th century, taking control of [[British Columbia]] and establishing the Falkland Islands colony. Most remaining colonies gained independence between 1962 and 1983, and many joined the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

American singer, known as the "Princess of Pop." Her debut single, "...Baby One More Time", topped the US Billboard Hot 100. Her song "Toxic" won a Grammy Award for Best Dance Recording. She became the third woman to top the Billboard Hot 100 in three separate decades. After an involuntary conservatorship, which ended in 2021, she announced her departure from the music industry in 2024. [[Forbes]] named her the world's highest-paid female musician in 2000 and 2012.

Peninsula, historical region and cultural area in northwestern France, and the traditional homeland of the Breton people. Brittany was an independent kingdom and then a duchy before it was united with the [[Kingdom of France]] in 1532, when it was governed as a separate nation under the crown. Its name, from Latin *Britannia*, reflects settlement by Cornish Britons after the fall of the [[Western Roman Empire]]. Brittany is one of six Celtic nations, and the Breton language was spoken daily by an estimated 107,000 people as of 2024. The region has some of the world's oldest standing architecture, including the Cairn of Barnenez, which dates to the early 5th millennium BC. A nationalist movement seeks greater autonomy within France or independence from it.

Mountain in the [[Karakoram]] range on the border of Pakistan and China, and the 12th-highest mountain on Earth. Its main summit rises to 8,051 metres (26,414 ft), and it lies about eight kilometres from [[K2]]. It is one of the eight-thousanders. The first ascent was made in June 1957 by an Austrian expedition. On March 5, 2013, a Polish team made the first winter ascent.

American semiconductor and infrastructure software company, headquartered in Palo Alto, California. Its products serve the data center, networking, broadband, wireless, storage and industrial markets. Revenue in 2025 came 58% from semiconductor-based products and 42% from infrastructure software and services. Avago Technologies changed its name to Broadcom in January 2016 in order to acquire Broadcom Corporation. The company completed its acquisition of VMware on November 22, 2023. Its market capitalization surpassed $2 trillion in April 2026.

Commercial theatre presented in the Theater District and at Lincoln Center along Broadway in Midtown Manhattan, New York City. Its 41 professional theaters each have 500 or more seats. Broadway and [[London]]'s West End together represent the highest commercial level of live theater in the English-speaking world. Most Broadway shows are musicals, and historian Martin Shefter argues that musicals culminating in the productions of [[Rodgers and Hammerstein]] became enormously influential forms of American popular culture. In the 2022–2023 season, Broadway shows sold about US$1.54 billion in tickets, and about 12.3 million people attended per season. Smaller venues are called off-Broadway, and those with fewer than 100 seats are called off-off-Broadway. The Tony Awards honor excellence in Broadway theatre.

Edible green plant of the [[Brassicaceae|cabbage family]], grown for its large flower heads and stalk. It belongs to the Italica cultivar group of *Brassica oleracea*, which also includes [[Cauliflower]], and it is a particularly rich source of [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]] and vitamin K. Its sulfur-containing compounds are diminished by boiling but are better preserved by steaming, microwaving or stir-frying. Broccoli was developed through breeding in the northern Mediterranean from about the sixth century BCE and spread to northern Europe by the 18th century. Italian immigrants brought it to North America in the 19th century. The name comes from the Italian plural of *broccolo*, meaning "the flowering crest of a cabbage."

Romantic drama film (2005) directed by [[Ang Lee]], adapted from Annie Proulx's 1997 short story. It follows two American cowboys, Ennis Del Mar and Jack Twist, from 1963 to 1983. Starring [[Heath Ledger]] and [[Jake Gyllenhaal]], it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, where it won the Golden Lion. The film won three [[Academy Awards]], including Best Director. Its loss to *Crash* for Best Picture drew considerable attention, and it grossed over $178 million worldwide against a $14 million budget.

Family of monocot flowering plants, known as bromeliads, with about 80 genera and 3,700 known species. Nearly all are native to the tropical Americas, with one species in tropical West Africa. The family includes epiphytes such as [[Spanish moss]] and terrestrial species such as the [[Pineapple]]. Many "tank bromeliads" store water in tanks formed by their tightly overlapping leaf bases, and some species are desert succulents. The largest is *Puya raimondii*, whose flower spike can reach 9–10 metres. The family is thought to have originated in the tepuis of the [[Guiana Shield]] about 100 million years ago. Many species use crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) photosynthesis, opening their stomata at night to reduce water loss.

Chemical element with the symbol Br and atomic number 35, a volatile red-brown liquid at standard conditions and a member of the [[Halogen|halogen]] group. Its properties lie between those of [[Chlorine]] and [[Iodine]]. The name derives from the Greek *bromos*, meaning "stench." It was isolated independently by Carl Jacob Löwig in 1825 and Antoine Jérôme Balard in 1826. Because it is very reactive, bromine does not occur free in nature, and it is extracted commercially from brine evaporation ponds, mostly in the United States and Israel. More than half of the bromine produced worldwide each year is used as fire retardants, and the pesticide methyl bromide is no longer used because of [[Ozone depletion]]. Bromine is an essential trace element for collagen development in all animals.

Inflammation of the bronchi, the large and medium-sized airways of the lungs, causing coughing. It usually begins as an infection of the nose, ears, throat or sinuses. Acute bronchitis, also called a chest cold, causes a cough that usually lasts about three weeks, and in more than 90% of cases the cause is a viral infection. Treatment typically involves rest, [[Paracetamol|paracetamol]] and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Chronic bronchitis is defined as a productive cough lasting three months or more per year for at least two years. [[Tobacco smoking]] is its most common cause, and many patients also have [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] (COPD). Treatment includes quitting smoking, vaccinations, rehabilitation, and inhaled bronchodilators and steroids.

Polish-born anthropologist and ethnologist whose fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands helped establish modern ethnography. He popularized participant observation as a method. His principal work, *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922), described the Kula ring, a ceremonial exchange system. He taught at the [[London School of Economics]], where he became chair in anthropology. When World War II broke out, he held an appointment at [[Yale University]] and remained in the United States. His diary from fieldwork in [[Melanesia]] and [[New Guinea]], published by his widow in 1967, has been criticized for its ethnocentric and egocentric nature. His psychological functionalism contrasted with the structural functionalism of A. R. Radcliffe-Brown.

Literary family of 19th-century England, associated with the village of Haworth in the West Riding of Yorkshire. Born to Patrick Brontë, a curate, the sisters Charlotte, Emily and Anne published poems and novels under the male pseudonyms Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. Charlotte's *Jane Eyre* was the first of their works to achieve success, while Emily's *Wuthering Heights* and Anne's *Agnes Grey* were accepted as masterpieces after their deaths. The early deaths of their mother and two elder sisters profoundly influenced their writing. [[Mary Shelley]]'s novel *The Last Man* has been shown to have influenced their juvenile work. Their Haworth parsonage is now the Brontë Parsonage Museum, which receives hundreds of thousands of visitors annually.

Most populous borough of [[New York City]], coextensive with Kings County, at the western end of Long Island. The borough had a population of 2,736,074 in the 2020 United States census. Founded by the Dutch in the 17th century, it was consolidated into New York City on January 1, 1898, after a long political campaign. Jews form around a fifth of its population. In the first decades of the 21st century, Brooklyn's renaissance as a destination for hipsters brought gentrification and a decrease in housing affordability. The borough is linked to [[Manhattan]] by bridges and tunnels, including the [[Brooklyn Bridge]].

Suspension bridge across the East River in New York City, linking [[Manhattan]] and [[Brooklyn]]. It opened on May 24, 1883, and was the first fixed crossing of the East River. When it opened it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, with a main span of 1,595.5 feet (486.3 m). John A. Roebling designed the bridge, and his son Washington Roebling oversaw construction, assisted by Washington's wife, the engineer Emily Warren Roebling. Construction began in 1870 and took over thirteen years. The bridge carried horse-drawn vehicles and elevated railway lines until 1950, and today it carries passenger vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists.
